title: Phoebe, Junia, and a Church of Names
summary: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchrea who is probably carrying the letter, and sends greetings to a long list of believers in Rome, including Prisca and Aquila, Andronicus and Junia, and many others. He warns against people who cause divisions and deceive the naive, promises that God will soon crush Satan, and passes on greetings from his companions in Corinth, including Timothy and his scribe Tertius. The letter ends with a doxology to the only wise God, who has revealed the mystery of the gospel for the obedience of faith among all nations.
story: After the long argument of chapters 1 to 11 and the practical teaching of chapters 12 to 15, the letter closes with people. The names in this chapter show what the gospel of Romans produced: a church in the empire's capital made up of Jews and Gentiles, men and women, slaves or freed slaves and householders, meeting in several homes. Paul had never visited Rome, yet he knew many of these believers from elsewhere, a reminder of how much early Christians traveled. The chapter also gives a glimpse of the network behind Paul's mission and of the prominent place of women within it.
historical:
Cenchrea (or Cenchreae) was Corinth's eastern port on the Saronic Gulf. Phoebe likely traveled from there to Rome with the letter and would have been able to explain it to the churches. Prisca (called Priscilla in Acts) and Aquila were a Jewish couple who had left Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews around AD 49, worked with Paul as tentmakers in Corinth, and hosted a church in Ephesus (Acts 18:1-3, 18-26; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Their presence in Rome again fits a return after Claudius's death in AD 54. Some have suggested that the household of Aristobulus (verse 10) refers to the household of a grandson of Herod the Great, and that the household of Narcissus (verse 11) refers to the slaves and freedmen of a powerful freedman of Claudius by that name, but these identifications cannot be confirmed. Rufus (verse 13) may be the son of Simon of Cyrene mentioned in Mark 15:21, since Mark's Gospel is traditionally connected with Rome, though the name was common.

The greetings from Corinth include Gaius, Paul's host (probably the Gaius baptized by Paul in 1 Corinthians 1:14), and Erastus, the city treasurer. An inscription found near the theater in Corinth names an Erastus who laid a pavement at his own expense in return for his office as a city official, and some scholars identify him with Paul's Erastus, though the offices described may not be the same. Tertius, who wrote the letter down at Paul's dictation, adds his own greeting. The manuscripts of Romans show that this final chapter circulated in different forms. Verse 24 is absent from the earliest manuscripts, and the doxology of verses 25 to 27 appears in different places in different copies.
cultural:
Letters in the ancient world often ended with greetings, and letters of recommendation were a common way of introducing a traveler to people who could offer help and hospitality. Paul's commendation of Phoebe is such a letter in miniature. Many of the names in the list, such as Ampliatus, Hermes, Nereus, and Julia, were common among slaves and freed slaves in Rome, so the list suggests a church drawn largely from ordinary and lower-status people. There were no church buildings; believers met in houses and apartment buildings, and Paul greets several household groups.

The "holy kiss" (verse 16) reflects a common custom of greeting family and friends with a kiss. Among believers it became a sign that they were family to one another, across lines of class and ethnicity. Phoebe is also called a prostatis, a word used in the Greek world for a patron or benefactor, someone who used wealth and standing to support others. Patrons were central to Roman society. Paul, who elsewhere refuses to be dependent on patrons, gladly acknowledges her help to many, including himself.
literary: The chapter is built of five parts: a commendation (verses 1-2), a long list of greetings sent by Paul (verses 3-16), a warning (verses 17-20), greetings from those with Paul (verses 21-23), and a closing doxology (verses 25-27). The verb for greeting appears twenty-one times in the chapter, giving the list a steady rhythm. Paul attaches descriptions to many names (fellow worker, beloved, worked hard, approved, chosen), so the list becomes a set of small portraits. The doxology echoes the letter's opening (1:1-5), with the gospel, the prophets, and the obedience of faith among all nations, so the letter ends where it began.

outline.t: A warning against those who cause divisions
Doxology to the only wise God

doctrines.note: The church is a family of named people, gathered in households, bound to one another in the Lord. Paul's greetings show that the church is made up of real people whose labor matters, not only of doctrines.
The doxology speaks of the mystery kept secret for long ages but now revealed through the prophetic writings and made known to all nations. God's plan was hidden and is now disclosed in the gospel.
Verse 20 promises that the God of peace will soon crush Satan under believers' feet, an echo of the promise in Genesis 3:15 that the offspring of the woman would crush the serpent's head.

words.note: Diakonos, servant or deacon. Paul uses it of himself, of Christ, of Apollos, and of government. In Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3:8-13 it names a recognized church office. Phoebe is called a diakonos of the church at Cenchrea, and translations are divided between servant and deacon. Many interpreters think the link to a particular church suggests a recognized role, while others take it in the general sense of one who serves.

Prostatis, patron or benefactor, the only use of the word in the New Testament. In Greek usage it described a person who protected and supported others, often through wealth and influence. It indicates that Phoebe was a woman of means and standing who used them for the church and for Paul.

Iounias, Junia. In the Greek accusative the name could in principle be accented as the female name Junia or as a male name Junias. Junia was a common Latin woman's name, while no ancient example of Junias as a man's name has been found. Early Christian writers took her as a woman, and most modern translations now read Junia.

Episemos, notable or outstanding. The phrase in verse 7 can be read as outstanding among the apostles (counting Andronicus and Junia as apostles) or well known to the apostles (esteemed by them). Grammatical studies have been cited on both sides.

christ: Christ is the center of the network Paul describes. Believers are "in Christ" or "in the Lord" again and again, the phrase that marks where their identity and relationships now lie. Andronicus and Junia were in Christ before Paul, and Epenetus was the first convert to Christ in Asia. The warning that some serve their own appetites rather than "our Lord Christ" (verse 18) shows that loyalty to Christ is the test of teaching. The promise that God will soon crush Satan under your feet draws on Genesis 3:15, which Christians have read as the first promise of the one who would defeat evil. The doxology says that God strengthens his people by the gospel and "the proclamation of Jesus Christ" and that glory belongs to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

hard.q: What do Phoebe and Junia tell us about the roles of women in the early church?
hard.a:
Romans 16 names at least ten women, and several are described in terms of ministry: Phoebe is a diakonos and a patron, Prisca is Paul's fellow worker and is named before her husband, and Mary, Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis have worked hard in the Lord. Two debates focus on specific verses. The first concerns Phoebe's title, diakonos, which can mean servant in a general sense or deacon in a recognized role. The second concerns Junia. For much of the medieval and modern period, some translations read a man's name, Junias, but the church writers of the first centuries took her as a woman, and most scholars today agree. The remaining question is whether verse 7 means she and Andronicus were outstanding among the apostles or well known to the apostles. Some scholars, notably Michael Burer and Daniel Wallace in a 2001 study, argued for the second reading; others have responded that the first is more natural. Even on the first reading, apostle here may mean a traveling missionary or church messenger (as in 2 Corinthians 8:23) rather than one of the Twelve.

Christians who hold that some church offices are reserved for men (complementarians) and those who hold that all offices are open to women (egalitarians) both appeal to this chapter. Complementarians note that Paul's commendations do not settle the question of elders and teaching authority, which they see addressed elsewhere. Egalitarians see in Phoebe and Junia evidence that women held recognized ministry and leadership roles in Paul's churches. This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians differ. What the chapter shows beyond dispute is that women were central to Paul's mission and that he honored their work by name.

questions: Paul's greetings are full of small descriptions: beloved, worked hard, approved, a mother to me. What would it mean to see the people in your church the way Paul saw these?
Many of these names belong to ordinary people who would otherwise be forgotten. Why do you think Paul took the time to name them?
Paul warns against those who cause divisions with smooth talk. How can a church stay welcoming while also guarding against teaching that divides?
